content:
The stage play "We Are the Happiest," which had its performance cancelled by the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, was brought to Japan by Mount Zero bookstore. Yesterday (the 16th), at Home/Work Village in Setagaya Ward, Tokyo, Japanese actors read out the translated script, and a creative symposium was also held, with playwright Chong Mui-ngam and actor Anthony Wong in attendance to share their insights, drawing over a hundred Hong Kong and Japanese audience members.

Mount Zero bookstore set up the limited-time bookshop "Summer Holiday in a Foreign Land" at Home/Work Village in Setagaya Ward, with activities including a two-day reading of "We Are the Happiest."

Enthusiastic audience response leads to added performance session

This performance was one of the key events of "Summer Holiday in a Foreign Land (異国の夏休み)," a limited-time bookshop opened in Tokyo from July to September by the now-suspended independent bookstore Mount Zero. It also marks another work by Chong Mui-ngam to be staged in Japan, following earlier productions such as "The Left Behind," and more recently "Thirty-fifth of May" and "Wild Boar."

Mount Zero bookstore manager Sharon described the opportunity for this performance as a "telepathic connection" with Chong Mui-ngam, as both hoped to bring good things to share in Japan, which led to this reading and symposium. Sharon had worried about ticket sales and did not dare book a venue that was too large, but over a hundred tickets for the first session sold out within two days, leading to a decision to add an extra session in the gymnasium at Home/Work Village, and those tickets also sold out completely within a few days.

Mount Zero bookstore manager Sharon said that she and Chong Mui-ngam shared a "telepathic connection" in their hope to bring good things to share in Japan, which led to this reading and symposium.

Translated and read by Japanese actors; Anthony Wong: Emotion has nothing to do with language

"We Are the Happiest" tells the story of a young gay male couple—articled barrister Philip and Ah Sang—whose relationship undergoes changes after the involvement of Philip's boss Neil, leading to a tragic ending. The play had its premiere in 2022 and was originally scheduled for a revival at the end of last year, but the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority said it had received complaints that the play "promoted confrontation and smeared Hong Kong," and cancelled the venue and performance.

For this production, Hong Kong-based director in Japan Indi Chan condensed the original roughly two-hour performance into one hour. Three Japanese actors—Egami Shingo (as Neil), Nakanishi Ryosuke (as Philip), and Kikuchi Kanki (as Ah Sang)—performed the translated Japanese text in reading format. After the reading, playwright Chong Mui-ngam and Anthony Wong, who was originally cast as Neil, joined the director and actors for a creative sharing session.

Three Japanese actors performed the translated Japanese text in reading format.

Among the ticket-holding audience, approximately one-third were Hong Kongers, with the rest being Japanese audience members. While watching the performance, many audience members opened Chinese or Japanese script collections to read along with the actors' reading, and Anthony Wong was among them. During the sharing session, he recalled that a teacher during his time at the Academy of Performing Arts once taught him that "emotion has nothing to do with language." He said this was his first time reading a Chinese script while following a performance in a foreign language, and was surprised that despite not understanding Japanese, he could follow the progress of the performance. He highly praised the outstanding performances of the three Japanese actors.

During the performance, many audience members, including Anthony Wong, opened Chinese or Japanese script collections to read along with the actors. He was surprised that despite not understanding Japanese, he could follow the progress of the performance, recalling that a teacher once taught him "emotion has nothing to do with language."

Anthony Wong also expressed hope that "We Are the Happiest" could have a formal performance in Japan, joking that he needs to learn Japanese and then play the youthful role in the play. In addition to the symposium, he also welcomed collaboration with Japanese arts sector professionals in areas such as performance. This time, he brought eight paintings to participate in "Summer Holiday in a Foreign Land," hoping to hold a solo painting exhibition in Japan next year.

Anthony Wong brought eight paintings copying Matisse to participate in "Summer Holiday in a Foreign Land," hoping to hold a solo painting exhibition in Japan next year.

Chong Mui-ngam: Gain experience from being banned; Anthony Wong: Immersive learning

When asked about the impact of being unable to stage her work in Hong Kong on her creative work, Chong Mui-ngam responded that public performances allow her to examine how text is presented, calling it "the final step in a playwright's learning process during creation." The inability to stage a production dealt a heavy blow to her, who loves the stage: "My emotions have been very up and down. I'm a bit happier now that I'm in Japan, but sometimes I feel really low." As for how she creates under such circumstances, she said she is still "adjusting," but she can continue writing even without being able to stage performances, and she is still working on new works.

Chong Mui-ngam drew on her experience of reading "Things in nature merely grow," sharing the resonance she felt with the author whose two sons died by suicide, emphasising that the experience of being banned had given her "a different feeling of understanding what others have gone through," and yielded "valuable experience." Anthony Wong described this as "immersive learning," drawing laughter from the audience. Chong Mui-ngam also laughed and said the description was very accurate, because "the setbacks you see are only the setbacks you see. In every aspect of my life, there are far more setbacks that you don't see." Anthony Wong responded by saying "I deeply empathise with your misfortune." Chong Mui-ngam stated frankly, "There are all kinds of setbacks today that you don't quite understand. One day in the future, I hope I can write them out," and said she would write them out together with Anthony Wong's share.

After the reading, playwright Chong Mui-ngam and Anthony Wong, who was originally cast as Neil in the play, joined the director and actors for a creative sharing session.

Chong Mui-ngam points to regression in situation for homosexuals; Anthony Wong uses cha-cha as metaphor

Nakanishi Ryosuke, who played Philip, said that participating in "We Are the Happiest" reminded him of "The Tale of Genji," a Japanese literary work from over a thousand years ago, in which characters who love but cannot have what they desire end up killing others or themselves. He had previously had doubts about these descriptions, but found that a thousand years later, this script from Hong Kong also contains the same plot, so he "began to somewhat understand this state of mind." Chong Mui-ngam explained that although the protagonist is homosexual, the exploration of the obsession with love and desire in the story is not limited by sexual orientation or national borders.

In response to the different performance location, Indi made changes to the original final act and added laws related to homosexuals in Hong Kong and Japan as background. At the sharing session, Indi mentioned that "whether in Hong Kong or Japan, same-sex couples are not able to marry under the law," calling on the audience to continue paying attention to their rights. Chong Mui-ngam said that in the area of homosexuality, she felt that Hong Kong had "regressed in many ways" compared with other places, and did not dare to say that the next generation would be more open; Anthony Wong used the cha-cha as a metaphor, saying that "the trajectory of social development is not a straight line," and that moving forward and backward is the norm.

An audience member wearing a commemorative T-shirt for "We Are the Happiest" asked questions of Anthony Wong and Chong Mui-ngam.

Audience: As long as it is a good work, there will always be people who appreciate it

Japanese audience Ms. Nakamura Moena had purchased tickets for the originally scheduled West Kowloon performance. After participating in the event, she said, "I am very happy to see the Japanese actors' interpretation in Tokyo, but it also brings back the feeling of being unable to see the performance in Hong Kong at that time." She said she was curious how Anthony Wong would play the role of Neil, and looked forward to having the opportunity to see a complete version of the stage performance in Japan.

Hong Kong audience Ms. So also purchased tickets for "We Are the Happiest," and specifically extended her stay in Japan to attend this symposium. Ms. So believes that this performance is an example of how there are still many people seeking different spaces to demonstrate their power: "As long as it is a good work, there will be people who appreciate it. Regardless of where it is or in what form, it can move others."
